title: Eagles Film Review: Analyzing Makai Lemon’s debut and other 53-man roster inclusions
summary: Thank goodness that is over. The next time I write one of these reviews, we will be discussing a real football game! This review will be shorter than usual and focuses on the players who survived cutdown day, either on the 53-man roster or the practice squad. The final preseason game is far more useful […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 28: Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver Makai Lemon #9 runs a route during the pre season game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Cincinnati Bengals on August 28th, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Thank goodness that is over. The next time I write one of these reviews, we will be discussing a real football game! This review will be shorter than usual and focuses on the players who survived cutdown day, either on the 53-man roster or the practice squad. The final preseason game is far more useful when viewed through that lens. I’ve also combined offense and defense because there was not much to look at. Makai Lemon’s first appearance was hardly spectacular. He caught three of his five targets for three yards, was targeted on Tanner McKee’s interception, and muffed a punt late in the game. However, I am not going to panic about a first-round receiver after one preseason appearance. I did not dislike this first route as much when I watched the All-22. On the TV copy, the release looked slow, but it looks better from a wide angle. Lemon has never been an outstanding separator against press coverage, and probably never will be, but his work at the line of scrimmage is good here. He beats the initial contact, gets on top of the cornerback, and puts himself in a position to win vertically. The problem comes at the top of the route. Lemon looks inside without selling the possibility that he is actually breaking in that direction, allowing the cornerback to read the route and make a play on the football. Obviously, it’s only one rep, but Lemon must become better at manipulating defensive backs once he has established leverage. Simply looking in one direction will not move NFL cornerbacks consistently. Still, arguably the difficult part of this rep is defeating press coverage and stacking the defender. Lemon does that well. It wasn’t an ideal debut, but it wasn’t a disastrous one. Very quick Eagles Offense/Defense All22 Thread vs. Bengals with some notes on the 53. 1) I didn't hate this Lemon route as much on the All22. He's never been a huge separator vs. press anyway, but I think he does a good job at the LOS beating the press and stacking the CB. At… pic.twitter.com/qlxmFldaNS — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 31, 2026 I have disliked how the Eagles handled the backup quarterback position throughout the summer. Rotating Andy Dalton, Tanner McKee, and Cole Payton prevented anyone from developing much rhythm, and McKee appears to have suffered most. He completed 12 of 22 passes for 55 yards and an interception in this game, finishing the preseason looking far less comfortable than expected. This rep highlights McKee’s biggest limitation. He is never going to create consistently outside structure, so once the original concept breaks down, he has to make a quick decision. This is why I’ve never seen him as a starter, and I never thought another team would trade for him to be their starter. He can climb the pocket and take the available yards here. Instead, he drifts around behind the line of scrimmage and attempts to manufacture something that is never there. McKee does not possess the movement skills to play this way. His strengths are anticipation, accuracy, and operating within structure. If the first read or passing concept is covered, he cannot suddenly turn into an improvisational quarterback. Plays like this explain why teams can view him as a valuable backup without believing he should be their starter. 2) I've hated how the Eagles have handled the backup QB position this year, as it doesn't seem to have done Tanner McKee any favors at all. He's had some rough reps all preseason and doesn't look comfortable. He is never going to be someone who creates out of structure, so if… pic.twitter.com/QexTjtZ3lx — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 31, 2026 Micah Morris making the roster was no surprise. He played all 60 offensive snaps against the Bengals and completed a strong preseason. The Eagles value offensive linemen who can play multiple positions, and Morris has enough size, movement ability, and technical quality to provide depth at guard and tackle. This is exactly the type of rep I look for during the preseason. All offensive linemen will lose at times. The important question is whether they can recover after the initial technique fails. Morris does not land his first punch cleanly, but he stays balanced, resets his hands, and prevents the rusher from taking control of the rep. Being able to reset your hands is so important. Recovery ability matters because NFL pass protection will rarely look perfect. Offensive linemen need enough athleticism and body control to survive after losing the first phase of a rep. Morris deserved to make the roster, and I’m happy for him. 3) Absolutely no surprise that Micah Morris (76) has made the roster. I always look for reps like this in preseason that show a player go through challenges within a rep. He doesn't land his initial punch well, but his recovery ability is excellent, which is something you want to… pic.twitter.com/s8RQ4cT5jq — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 31, 2026 Morris and Jake Majors work together extremely well on this run. They create movement at the point of attack before Morris climbs to the second level, and both linemen remain controlled throughout the rep. Majors played 46 offensive snaps and finished an excellent preseason. He never had much chance of making the roster because of the Eagles’ depth along the interior offensive line, but bringing him back on the practice squad was an obvious decision. He looked comfortable for an undrafted free agent and gives the Eagles another developmental center who can also play guard. I’m happy no one picked him up! The one offensive line decision that upset me was losing Cameron Williams. The Falcons claimed him after the Eagles waived him . I have always been a fan of his upside. He remains raw, but offensive tackles with his size, length, and movement ability are difficult to find. I would have preferred to retain Williams and continue developing him over keeping an extra QB. He may never become a starter, yet his physical ceiling made him worth protecting. The Eagles kept Fred Johnson over him, which I understand (Markel Bell has been injured), and the overall offensive line depth remains strong. Williams is still the one loss I feel sad about. But I’m biased, because I was a fan pre-draft; you can’t help who you like! 4) Excellent blocks here by Micah Morris (76) and Jake Majors (75). I feel for Majors, as he had an excellent preseason but had no chance at making the 53 due to the Eagles' depth at the interior of the offensive line. I hope Majors sticks around on the practice squad, as he's… pic.twitter.com/o5Jhg6OFxI — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) August 31, 2026 On to the defense, this was another encouraging coverage rep from Kelee Ringo. I criticized his performance earlier in the preseason because he continues to look uncomfortable playing off coverage, so it is only fair to highlight the good plays too. The route initially looks like it could break outside, but Ringo does not overcommit. He keeps his hips under control, maintains his positioning, and reacts quickly once the receiver declares. His size and closing speed allow him to attack the catch point and prevent the completion. This is the version of Ringo the Eagles need. His technique will never look as fluid as some smaller cornerbacks, but he has rare physical tools. If he can avoid opening his hips prematurely and trust his recovery speed, he can survive in off coverage. He should enter the season as the first outside cornerback off the bench. 5) Onto the defense. I credited Kelee Ringo's play last week, and this is another excellent rep to see. You'd expect an out route here, but Ringo does a good job not overcommitting, staying in position, and…

title: Eagles jersey number updates: New look for Cole Payton and others
summary: Following recent NFL roster cuts, multiple Philadelphia Eagles players capitalized on being able to change to newly available jersey numbers. Here’s a very important update for you since I’m the definitive authority on all things related to #JerseyNumberAnalytics. OVERVIEW CHANGES ON THE ROSTER QB Cole Payton — from No. 10 to No. 18 CB Jonathan […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 22: Cole Payton #10 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL preseason football game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Following recent NFL roster cuts, multiple Philadelphia Eagles players capitalized on being able to change to newly available jersey numbers. Here’s a very important update for you since I’m the definitive authority on all things related to #JerseyNumberAnalytics. OVERVIEW CHANGES ON THE ROSTER QB Cole Payton — from No. 10 to No. 18 CB Jonathan Jones — from No. 32 to No. 31 LS Rocco Underwood — from No. 37 to No. 41 CHANGES ON INJURED RESERVE S Andre’ Sam — from No. 31 to No. 32 PRACTICE SQUAD: CHANGES AND NEW ADDITIONS RB Jaydon Blue — No. 30 CB Robert Longerbeam — No. 38 EDGE Mason Reiger — No. 43 OL Kiran Amegadjie — No. 73 WR Britain Covey — from No. 18 to No. 85 … Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. JERSEY NUMBER ANALYTICS COLE PAYTON Payton was previously sharing No. 10 with Eagles punter Braden Mann. Having two players with the same jersey numbers is allowed during the offseason when there’s up to 90 spots on the roster. But it’s obviously not permitted in the regular season. And so either Payton or Mann had to change … and it’s not surprising to see the onus was on the fourth-string rookie quarterback. Payton is the first Eagles quarterback to wear No. 18 since Josh McCown last did in 2019. I liked No. 10 for Payton more than I like No. 18. But now he wear the same number that Peyton Manning used to sport. Therefore: Cole Payton Manning. Boom. Hall of Fame trajectory. JONATHAN JONES Jones dropped down one number to go back to the No. 31 he’s worn since entering the league in 2016. Entirely sensible decision. He’ll be a cromulent option if he has to play. ROCCO UNDERWOOD Underwood and his fellow undrafted rookie Tucker Large, who is on the reserve/non-football injury list, were sharing No. 37 this offseason. Maybe not the best sign for Underwood that he’s the one who had to change? But I’m guessing it’s actually the long snapper who wanted to change to No. 41 — which was previously held by Tariq Castro-Fields — to be one number away from his college look at Florida: No. 42. Long snapper numbers are typically never pretty so No. 41 is fine for Underwood. ANDRE’ SAM Sam suffered what seemed to be a season-ending injury during the Eagles’ final preseason game … and now he doesn’t at least get to keep his number while on injured reserve?! Poor guy. Hope he was able to get some money or something from Jonathan Jones to flip from No. 31 to No. 32. Maybe Sam is just so much of a team guy that he wanted Jones to have it. JAYDON BLUE Blue wore No. 34 during the preseason last year. Then he changed to No. 23 in the regular season as a rookie, which is the same number he wore at Texas. That’s too flashy of a number for being one of three running backs on the practice squad. No. 30 is a more humble look for him. Also like a non-20s number for a smaller guy who profiles in part as a pass-catching back. ROBERT LONGERBEAM Much like Longerbeam might have to bide his time to find snaps on the Eagles (given that he has six cornerbacks ahead of him on the roster), he will have to be patient and wait until a better jersey number becomes available. No. 38 was previously worn by Ambry Thomas, who was not very good this summer prior to getting cut. Longerbeam previously wore No. 37 with the Ravens after wearing No. 7 at Rutgers. Maybe Longerbeam takes No. 7 after Kelee Ringo potentially leaves the Eagles in free agency after the 2026 season. MASON REIGER Previously held by Jose Ramirez (who just signed to the New England Patriots’ practice squad ), No. 43 is a tough one. He wore No. 22 in college, which isn’t a bad number by any means, but it’s not a fit for an edge rusher. He then had No. 90 with the Miami Dolphins earlier this year. Reiger will have to prove he eventually deserves an upgrade. He should aim for No. 97, which will be open after Moro Ojomo signs a huge contract with another team in March 2027. KIRAN AMEGADJIE Amegadjie wore No. 72 with Yale and the Chicago Bears. With Markel Bell already holding that number in Philly, he’s moving up a number to take the No. 73 left behind by Cameron Williams. Totally acceptable look for his developmental tackle role. BRITAIN COVEY Covey was a victim of Payton having to change out of No. 10. The rookie quarterback took No. 18 to force Covey into No. 85, which he briefly had after rejoining the team last year. Too big of a number for such a small receiver. Stock down. If the Eagles decide to stop keeping four quarterbacks, Covey might look to go after No. 14 (Andy Dalton) or No. 16 (Tanner McKee)? Or maybe Payton could take one of those numbers and Covey could get No. 18 back?

full_text: PHOENIX, AZ - DECEMBER 26: Rutgers Scarlet Knights defensive back Robert Longerbeam (7) reacts to a big play during the Rate Bowl college football game between the Rutgers Scarlet Knights and the Kansas State Wildcats on December 26, 2024 at Chase Field in Phoenix, Arizona. (Photo by Kevin Abele/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles are signing four more players to fill out their practice squad, according to an official team announcement. This development comes one day after the team initially signed 13 practice squad players . Here’s an overview of the new additions: WR Danny Gray OL Kiran Amegadjie CB Robert Longerbeam RB Jaydon Blue The Eagles now have 17 players on the practice squad, which is normally limited to a 16-player capacity … but Uar Bernard is able to join on an international exemption. Let’s sort through the latest news on a player-by-player basis. DANNY GRAY Gray originally joined the Eagles in September 2024. He was waived by the team last July before returning to Philly’s practice squad in November 2025. Gray spent the entire 2026 offseason with the Eagles. He’s been a solid practice player. Totally acceptable depth option to keep around. KIRAN AMEGADJIE The Amegadjie (ah-muh-GAHD-jee) signing was first reported on Monday . A 2024 third-round pick (No. 75 overall) by the Chicago Bears, Amegadjie logged 123 offensive snaps as a rookie (119 at left tackle, four at left guard) over one start made in six games played. He then missed the 2025 season due to injury. Amegadjie played 104 snaps at left tackle and 13 at right tackle in the preseason this summer before the Bears waived him. With the Eagles losing 2025 draft picks Myles Hinton and Cameron Williams to waivers, it doesn’t hurt to add a new long-levered developmental tackle option. Especially with Lane Johnson potentially retiring after 2026. We’ll see if Chris Kuper can help him eventuallyl fulfill his potential. Pre-draft scouting report via NFL.com’s Lance Zierlein : With a rare blend of athletic traits and eye-popping length, it might be a mistake to bet against the high number of boxes Amegadjie checks. His hand usage is a work in progress, and he hasn’t learned to consistently get into blocks with proper footwork and body control, but both issues are coachable and likely to be corrected. Provided he improves his punch-timing and placement, his ability to keep rushers at the end of his length could become a big advantage. Amegadjie already possesses impressive explosiveness as a drive blocker and could become a quality NFL starter once his tutelage is complete. Spider graph via Mockdraftable : ROBERT LONGERBEAM First of all, great name. I sure would hate to be Robert Longbeam. Longerbeam, who turns 26 in January, was a fifth-round pick (No. 212 overall) by the Baltimore Ravens in the 2025 NFL Draft after playing college football at Rutgers. He missed his entire rookie season due to a knee injury before making some noise in training camp/preseason games this summer. According to Pro Football Focus charting, Longerbeam allowed just an 84.2 passer rating while targeted in coverage. He finished the preseason as the Ravens’ third-best defender by PFF grading. In a recent roundtable article over at Baltimore Beatdown , multiple Ravens writers brought up Longerbeam as a player they were concerned about getting claimed on waivers: DUSTIN COX: Longerbeam had a very strong preseason in his rebound from a season-ending injury that derailed his rookie season before it began last year. He deserved to make the roster, but the Ravens had too many quality cornerbacks ahead of him. Cornerback depth is of utmost importance in the NFL, so it would not surprise me to see someone claim Longerbeam. ZACH CANTER: Lastly, cornerback Robert Longerbeam finally had a chance to show what he could do after suffering an injury during his rookie year last preseason. He showed great coverage and open field tackling ability and I think a team would be lucky to grab him as depth. But hopefully the Ravens can sneak last years draft pick back on their practice squad. The Eagles currently have six cornerbacks on their 53-man roster: Quinyon Mitchell, Cooper DeJean (nickel CB who will also play at safety), Riq Woolen, Jonathan Jones, Kelee Ringo, and Mac McWilliams. It’s easy to feel great about the starting trio of Q, Coop, and Woolen. The depth behind them is less inspiring. Jones is versatile and experienced but the soon-to-be 33-year-old missed most of training camp due to injury. Ringo is more easily trusted to help on special teams than he is to contribute on defense. It was a little surprising to see McWilliams made the roster because he struggled in the preseason games and was up and down in training camp practices. Adding Longerbeam to the mix gives the Eagles another potential depth option. He’s mostly spent time at outside corner but there’s thought he could be moved inside due to his frame. Definitely worth taking a chance on his upside. Pre-draft scouting report via NFL.com’s Lance Zierlein : Slender cornerback who is “wired right” but lacks the size NFL teams typically require. Longerbeam played outside at Rutgers, but the size disadvantage likely means he’ll be moving inside as a pro. He has the feet to match route breaks and good burst to close from zone. He gives some ground deep and struggles to win above the rim, though. He’s a willing run supporter but the frame will only allow so much. His on-ball production and competitiveness are appealing, but teams will need to balance those elements against his size when determining his draft value. Spider graph via Mockdraftable : JAYDON BLUE News of the Eagles signing Blue first emerged on Monday night. It’s a little curious to see the Eagles add a third running back to the practice squad (to join Dameon Pierce and Carson Steele) while also having three on the roster (Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, and Will Shipley). That being said, using a practice squad spot on Blue feels worthwhile. The Birds hosted him on a pre-draft visit last year before he was selected by the Dallas Cowboys with a fifth-round pick (No. 149 overall) in the 2025 NFL Draft. Blue played just 78 offensive snaps for the Cowboys as a rookie, logging 38 carries for 129 yards (3.4 average) and one touchdown. His sole target resulted in a five-yard reception. During the 2026 preseason, Blue produced 94 rushing yards on 23 attempts (4.1 average) in addition to two catches for 15 yards. The Cowboys waived Blue while originally only keeping two running backs (plus one fullback) on their roster before claiming Emari Demercado off waivers from the Kansas City Chiefs to be their new RB3. Now in Philly, Blue will have a chance to develop behind the scenes. Scouting report via NFL.com’s Lance Zierlein : Blue played behind very good backs, so his carry count is lower, but he clearly has talent. He’s a narrow-hipped, linear runner with good speed to threaten wide and attack downfield out of the backfield. He has adequate wiggle in the open field but lacks base strength to break tackles. Blue’s lack of tempo and vision inside gets him behind schedule and could limit how teams use him as a ball-carrier. While he can be labeled a “change-of-pace slasher,” his real value will revolve around his ability to mismatch linebackers and threaten defenses as a receiver out of the backfield. Spider graph via Mockdraftable: EAGLES PRACTICE SQUAD As a refresher, here’s the Eagles’ entire practice squad. OL Kiran Amegadjie RB Jaydon Blue LB Chance Campbell WR Britain Covey WR Danny Gray DT Gabe Hall EDGE Keyshawn James-Newby CB Robert Longerbeam C/G Jake Majors OT John Ojukwu RB Dameon Pierce S Maximus Pulley EDGE Mason Reiger RB Carson Steele EDGE Joshua Weru S Cole Wisniewski International exemption: DT Uar Bernard

Teams had until Sunday at 6:00 PM Eastern to make their roster cuts . At 1:00 PM on Monday, August 31, any claims for players on the waiver wire will be revealed. Still, after players are claimed, teams can then fill their 16-man practice squads. Keep track of the Eagles roster/practice squad moves below. Can the Eagles be patient with Makai Lemon and Eli Stowers? – Inquirer “Tremendous confidence in who those guys are as players, what their skill set is. Obviously, they had some setbacks here physically and we looked at that as a staff and a group and maybe can figure out some changes here to get those guys going a little bit sooner from a skill position perspective. But don’t have any doubt about what they’re going to be in the NFL over time. Still believe they’re going to contribute to our 2026 team.” That may end up the case. But Roseman’s 53-man roster construction suggests he went deeper at receiver and tight end than he did a year ago to account for Lemon’s and Stowers’ stunted starts. Moore, as the sixth receiver, could shoulder some of the load on concepts designed for Lemon if he struggles early. But Roseman seems to want to follow his own advice, which is to be patient. And that may apply to the new offensive system as much as it does the youngsters. Coordinator Sean Mannion kept his cards close in camp, joint practices, and the preseason. But the offense was objectively scattershot. Practice Squad Moves and Roster Talk – Iggles Blitz The Eagles did add some outside players. OT Kiran Amegadjie was a third round pick of the Bears. He struggled mightily in pass pro, but showed promise as a run blocker. We’ll see if the Eagles can do a better job of developing him than Chicago did. Edge rusher Mason Reiger is a high motor player who is a good fit for the Eagles scheme. RB Jaydon Blue comes over from Dallas. Eagles GM Howie Roseman on Uar Bernard, lack of trades, more – NBCSP Risking Bernard and Weru. The Eagles took a gamble this weekend by waiving International Pathway Program players DT Uar Bernard and OLB Joshua Weru. But that gamble paid off because both cleared waivers and have since been signed to the Eagles’ practice squad. “We’re not sitting there and cutting anyone and going, ‘Woohoo, this guy, we’re definitely getting back,’” Roseman said. “You don’t know what other teams are thinking.” During training camp, defensive coordinator Vic Fangio did everything he could to temper expectations for Bernard and Weru. title: Steelers’ Joey Porter Jr. doesn’t close door on sitting out Week 1
summary: Three players from the Steelers’ 2023 draft class received big-money extensions from the team this offseason. Not among that group was arguably the best player in that Pittsburgh draft class: cornerback Joey Porter Jr., who didn’t practice over the summer while on the Physically Unable to Perform list with a reported back injury — and […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Joey Porter Jr. #24 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on during the game against the Green Bay Packers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Three players from the Steelers’ 2023 draft class received big-money extensions from the team this offseason. Not among that group was arguably the best player in that Pittsburgh draft class: cornerback Joey Porter Jr., who didn’t practice over the summer while on the Physically Unable to Perform list with a reported back injury — and while hoping for a new contract himself in a competitive cornerback market. Speaking to the media after his first practice since being activated from the PUP list on Sunday, Porter said he “didn’t know” when asked if he would play Week 1 without a new contract, when Pittsburgh will open the season against the Atlanta Falcons on Sept. 13. “I have to talk to the guys upstairs, my agents about that one,” he said, according to ESPN’s Brooke Pryor . At a different point, when asked if he would play if healthy, Porter responded, “Yeah, for sure… maybe,” according to The Athletic’s Mike DeFabo . “I really can’t speak much to the future, but today, I was out there today, running with the guys,” Porter said via Steelers Now’s Alan Saunders . “Still trying to get back fully.” Before Tuesday’s practice, Steelers’ head coach Mike McCarthy noted the star corner was still “ ramping up ” after spending time on the PUP list. Porter is entering the last season of his rookie deal. Earlier this offseason, the Seahawks’ Devon Witherspoon reset the cornerback market with a $33 million average-per-year extension.

title: Mike McCarthy explains why Steelers released Elandon Roberts
summary: One of the Steelers’ most unexpected moves on roster cutdown day was the decision to release veteran linebacker Elandon Roberts. Talking to the media on Tuesday, Pittsburgh head coach Mike McCarthy was asked to explain the reasoning in cutting Roberts, who signed with the team in mid-August. McCarthy emphasized special teams ability in his response, […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - JANUARY 11: Elandon Roberts #50 of the Pittsburgh Steelers rushes the passer during an NFL football wild card playoff game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on January 11, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the Steelers’ most unexpected moves on roster cutdown day was the decision to release veteran linebacker Elandon Roberts. Talking to the media on Tuesday, Pittsburgh head coach Mike McCarthy was asked to explain the reasoning in cutting Roberts, who signed with the team in mid-August. McCarthy emphasized special teams ability in his response, a phase of the game Roberts saw little playing time in over the summer despite a heavy dose of preseason reps. “Number one, an outstanding player. (Roberts) came here late. He’s definitely up to his reputation,” McCarthy said, according to PennLive’s Nick Farabaugh . “You know, I enjoyed him while he was here. I wish him the best of luck. But there’s a lot of things that go into those final decisions. You know, special teams is usually a big part of that once you get passed through the first 11 or 12 going out on the field, offense and defense.” After cutdown day, Roberts said he was “ shocked ” by Pittsburgh’s decision. According to Dejan Kovacevic of DK Pittsburgh Sports, there was no handshake agreement to bring Roberts back at some point, and the linebacker was not signed to the team’s initial practice squad . However, speaking to the media on Monday, team general manger Omar Khan said that the team was “certainly not closing the door” on a reunion with the fan-favorite run stuffer. “I have a lot of respect for E-Rob,” Khan said. “We have some history with him, and he’s done a good job. Love the player and love the person.”

title: Joey Porter Jr. to return to practice Tuesday for Steelers
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers are under two weeks away from taking the field for their season opener at Acrisure Stadium against the Atlanta Falcons. However, one issue still hanging over the Steelers is the contract “impasse” with cornerback Joey Porter Jr. While no reports suggest a deal is close to being done, Porter Jr. will be […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - JANUARY 12: Joey Porter Jr. #24 of the Pittsburgh Steelers defends in coverage during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Houston Texans at Acrisure Stadium on January 12, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers are under two weeks away from taking the field for their season opener at Acrisure Stadium against the Atlanta Falcons. However, one issue still hanging over the Steelers is the contract “impasse” with cornerback Joey Porter Jr. While no reports suggest a deal is close to being done, Porter Jr. will be back on the practice field this week. After being activated from the PUP list after missing the entirety of training camp with a back injury, Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy said that Porter Jr. will “definitely” practice on Tuesday. “Anybody that comes in here for the first time, there’s a ramp-up type of process to it,” McCarthy said to the media. “That’s what we’ll look for with Joey today.” Steelers coach Mike McCarthy said Joey Porter Jr. "definitely" will practice today after being taken off PUP. "Anybody that comes in here for the first time, there's a ramp up type of process to it. That's what we'll look for with Joey today." — Mike DeFabo (@MikeDeFabo) September 1, 2026 When asked if Porter Jr. has done enough work off to the side during training camp to be ready to play up to speed in week one, McCarthy seemed to think that this “ramp up” process will give us some insight into the corners potential week one status. “Well, that’s why you have ramp-up. He’s been working with the medical people, so there’s definitely a process and there’s an understanding of what he was going through there with the injuries. There’s a process that every one of these players has gone through as far as ramping up before you go full speed on the field. So he’ll be in that category.” While it is an encouraging sign that Porter Jr. is returning to the practice field this week, this situation is far from over. Just over the weekend, ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported that Porter Jr. is upset that the Steelers have paid other players from the 2023 draft class before him. It doesn’t make financial sense for Porter Jr. to sit out and miss any of the regular season even if he doesn’t have a new deal from Pittsburgh. While the Steelers star corner is still unhappy with his contract situation, he is abiding by the McCarthy rule that if you are healthy, you are expected to practice. full_text: Welcome to the first Pittsburgh Steelers live chat of the 2026 season. With preseason and final roster cuts complete, we are just over one week away from the season kicking off with the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks facing off in the opening contest of the season. With the new year kicking off, we’ll begin our year of weekly one-hour live chats with your questions and comments. If you can’t make it each week for the lunchtime chats, you can always submit questions ahead of time in the callout post in The Feed., which one reader did this week. Steelers live chat question submissions Q: If Dean and Porter are our two starting outside cbs, who is first and second in line for slot corner duties? If Ramsey does or does not play safety, what is the order? And who is the primary backup for outside cb? Thanks for your hard work to all at BTSC . – jomac A: Ramsey would be the top nickel CB. (Photo by Randy Litzinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers have yet to reach a deal with cornerback Joey Porter on a long-term extension. As the regular season looms with the Steelers’ first game just 12 days away at the time of writing, the clock is ticking to get a deal done. The Steelers traditionally do not negotiate contracts once the regular season starts – something general manager Omar Khan says won’t be changing with Porter. “We won’t talk publicly about the negotiations per se, but Joey knows how we feel about him, and I still hope Joey finishes his career here,” Khan said via Brooke Pryor . “… Our policy is going to remain in place, but I’m not going to talk about negotiations.” Several cornerbacks have gotten paid this offseason, including Porter’s fellow 2023 draft classmate Devon Witherspoon, who is currently the highest-paid cornerback in the league on a per-year basis at $33 million. Denzel Ward also saw his salary increase to $31.1 million per year, and Trent McDuffie of the Rams is sitting at $31 million. Upon returning to practice, fellow Steelers cornerback Jalen Ramsey defended Porter and said the Steelers need to pay him. “We need the whole secondary,” Ramsey said via Nick Farabaugh of PennLive . “They need to pay Joey Porter Jr… “I’m overly in Joey’s corner. Joey needs to get compensated for being a valuable part of this secondary and a valuable part of this defense and team.” Should the Steelers reach an agreement with Porter, it would mark four players from their 2023 draft class that were given second contracts. title: How special teams is reflected in the Seahawks’ initial 53-man roster
summary: When special teams for the Seattle Seahawks is brought up, it’s easy to think names like Rashid Shaheed and Tory Horton. These two delivered some electric and vintage performances on the way to a championship. There were a few. If you’re a ball-knower, Michael Dickson might be your guy. Nick Kallerup, Eric Saubert, and Brady […]
full_text: When special teams for the Seattle Seahawks is brought up, it’s easy to think names like Rashid Shaheed and Tory Horton. These two delivered some electric and vintage performances on the way to a championship . There were a few. If you’re a ball-knower, Michael Dickson might be your guy. Nick Kallerup, Eric Saubert, and Brady Russell also figure to be versatile and tough components of advancing the ball on teams. This team doesn’t play about “the 3rd phase.” HBO’s Hard Knocks director, Pat Harris, called the Seattle Seahawks, “the best in the biz, right now” on The Official Hard Knocks Podcast last week. It is true that we are getting an unprecedented look at the inner workings of an elite sports organization, but the Hawks continue to produce documentary series that shed more and more light on how things tick. The Seattle Seahawks’ media team released a 3-episode installment entitled, “The Specialists.” It documents Jason Myers (he who set a record for most points scored in a single season in NFL history after five Super Bowl FG’s), Rashid Shaheed (Pro Bowl return man) and Michael Dickson (2nd-team, All-Pro punter). Mike Macdonald said of the importance the Seahawks organization places on special teams: “You got to back it up with your actions. So, it’s how you invest in it. It’s who you have out there, it’s who you have coaching them.” In hearing from one of those coaches that is most directly responsible ( Specialists, episode 2 ), we learned what he sees as valuable. Special teams coach, Jay Harbaugh says, “What makes a special teams unit great? You could go on and on and on about that… All the things that would make a defense or an offense great, combined into one. Shaheed, moments later, stated that in 2025, “Special teams was our edge.” Brandon Pili and Connor O’Toole are both on this roster, and they combined for a big turnover in season last year. Harbaugh has not forgotten about the defensive guys in discussing the role of “teams,” which “incorporates both offense and defense, [it’s] interesting to observe different techniques.” As we continue to study who made the 53-man roster, it’s very much worth considering special teams value. The Seahawks certainly do. The Seahawks spend more on their special teams than any other team in the NFL at $9.325M in salary. Their kicker just scored over half the points and their punter downed a punt inside the five-yard-line as Seattle won the Super Bowl. — Front Office Sports (@FOS) February 9, 2026 As far as Mike Macdonald’s defensive scheme goes, in a 3-4 defense, which (presumably) utilizes two off-ball LBs on the field at once, the Hawks kept five. Seattle doesn’t usually rotate that position either. If you play some of the Madden football games, only three will ever really get snaps in a lot of scenarios. This isn’t Madden, but they only kept three on the initial roster last year . Keeping five inside linebackers took away from their ability to keep guys like Jared Ivey (Atlanta), Noah Igbinoghene (Cleveland), Cody White (Las Vegas) and Jamie Sheriff (Los Angeles Rams and their “super team”). That’s an idea worth addressing. Macdonald did discuss finding a role for snaps on defense for Tyrice Knight: “it’s a good problem to have, from a coach’s perspective, of trying to figure out a way to get him out there, and what’s best for the team.” Could he replace a current starter, or is it more likely they find a unique role for him? Emmanwori plays a unique role, but this team likes to have multiple guys who can fill those niche positions. Think D’Anthony Bell backing up E-Man, t times. Think both Leo Williams and “The Polar Bear” (Rylie Mills, a nickname revealed to us by “Big Cat” during one of the preseason games) lining up at DT, but also EDGE at times. Think of both Mike Morris, as well as Jared Ivey playing big-bodied ends, but moonlighting on the interior of the defensive line at times. Think both Knight and Drake Thomas taking snaps on the outside edge of the defense. Shaheed, a former UDFA who made the Saints’ roster, went on later, in his episode of “The Specialists,” to state plainly: “It’s not everybody’s dream to be on special teams, but it’s always a dream to play in the NFL.” Whether a new LB role (that pulls in Knight, as well as other candidates) emerges or not, Morris, Patrick O’Connell and Chazz Surratt will be invaluable members of the Seattle Seahawks special teams squads as defensive guys. The linebackers, in particular might offer unique instincts, football intelligence, and physicality. That could be the biggest reason that it seems Seattle loaded up at that position. I mean, go back up top and click on the hyperlink “electric”, and you’ll see Surratt throw a key block on Horton’s punt return TD against the Saints. Side note : it may not be the first thing that comes to mind, even on special teams, but I hope there is an episode that gets added later, covering long snapper, Chris Stoll. After the Super Bowl win, Mike Dicko, the kicker said : “Oh yeah, Stoley… he’s the best in the world. He — some of the snaps today just felt like a video game. They came out so perfectly”. He went on to talk about the difficulty of his task, saying, “to be upside-down and be able to throw a ball backwards through the air to a spot this big brings his hands together to form a circle .” These special teamers deserve more of our respect for what they do outside of the limelight.

title: ‘Hard Knocks’: Seattle Seahawks season finale recap, highlights, and what we learned
summary: The season finale of “Hard Knocks” provided a perfect conclusion to the season in that it was all but conclusory. Throughout the episode, the impending “cut-down day” of the NFL season is approaching. Typically, this can be a very finite moment for players – either you made the roster or you didn’t. However, as the […]
full_text: The season finale of “Hard Knocks” provided a perfect conclusion to the season in that it was all but conclusory. Throughout the episode, the impending “cut-down day” of the NFL season is approaching. Typically, this can be a very finite moment for players – either you made the roster or you didn’t. However, as the Seattle Seahawks like to put it, cut-down day is “not doom and gloom. It’s stay strong and keep faith.” The path to repeating starts here 🏆 Thanks for watching Hard Knocks pic.twitter.com/EFWEXwVDoM — NFL Films (@NFLFilms) September 2, 2026 Staying strong and keeping the faith on the individual level mirrors what the team needs to do to reach the goal for 2026, to raise the Lombardi Trophy once again. Perhaps that mindset is exactly why “Hard Knocks” chose to end the final scene with Sam Darnold walking off the field breathing loudly and staying the course . Seattle is a place where individuals can flourish, and as a result, the team as a whole is able to grow. With that being said, let’s take a look at some of the best moments from the “Hard Knocks” season finale. The Seahawks 'baptized that chicken' on #Hardknocks #NFL #seahawks pic.twitter.com/vuCiU46um8 — Tanner Phifer (@TannerPhifer) September 2, 2026 Mike Macdonald starts the episode in his coaches meeting, reminding the staff that cut-down day is looming and to be cognizant that this is a tough time of the season for many players. Macdonald emphases that the message from coaches needs to be that everyone is on a different timetable as to their development. The Seahawks are shown how to “baptize that chicken” with the help of chef and food influencer Bernard Hardison. Derick Hall is shown enjoying the baptized chicken, while Uso Seumalo gives the feast a 9.7/10 rating. "Hard Knocks" was an accurate, authentic and entertaining look who the Seahawks are and how they operate. Wouldn't have been complete without a scene at Dino's. Also, not that you can go wrong with any Soundgarden song, but I respect going with a deep cut ("Dusty") at the end. https://t.co/PcFS4RKKmK — Brady Henderson (@BradyHenderson) September 2, 2026 John Schneider takes us to Dino’s Pub , where it is easier to have a difficult conversation over a beer. Schneider is joined by Head Strength and Conditioning coach, Ivan Lewis, and V.P. of Player Affairs, Maurice Kelly. Schneider describes the tough part about this time of the year, where on one hand you are preparing for the Week 1 opponent, New England Patriots, while on the other hand you have to figure out the best way to put together the best 70-man roster to help handle the “war of attrition” that the NFL is. Nick Emmanwori sees the light at the end of the tunnel in regards to his ankle injury. We see Emmanwori discussing his recovery with Coach Macdonald. Macdonald reminds Emmanwori not to worry about guys thinking he isn’t trying his hardest to get back. The “guys know who’s trying and who’s not.” Coach Macdonald hypes the team up ahead of the final preseason matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs by showing the team highlights from Uso Seumalo, Montorie Foster Jr., Jalen Milroe. He reminds Milroe again to “take out the Ferrari.” Jalen Milroe meets with quarterback coach, Jake Peetz. Peetz talks about how this game against the Chiefs will be a perfect chance for Milroe to prove himself as he will play the entire game and even get reps against the Chiefs A-team. Peetz reminds Milroe to keep it as simple as possible. It isn’t an episode of “Hard Knocks” without Derick Hall talking about his shorts. Hall pokes fun at Trevon Diggs, saying that Diggs’ legs are too little to wear short shorts and that he needs to put some shorts on that go down to his knees. There is a fun meeting between Diggs and his former college coach, turned defensive backs coach, Karl Scott. Scott shows Diggs some old tape of him at Alabama and tells Diggs not to forget who you are – “you always had legs, hope you still got ‘em.” Hard Knocks got an inside look at the meeting where the new @Seahawks owners were officially approved. The season finale of Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @Seahawks airs tonight at 9PM ET @hbomax pic.twitter.com/8CA8Jz8QbK — NFL (@NFL) September 1, 2026 They show the NFL owners meeting in Atlanta , where Vinod Khosla is officially voted in as the new owner of the Seattle Seahawks by a vote of 32-0. John Schneider is seen laughing when Khosla says that the plan is “simple”, to win another Super Bowl. Leonard Williams gets some “Love” when talking about his new three-year, $90 million extension. Williams talks with Julian Love about how they will have played 10 years together by the time his new contract is up – and with two separate teams (referring to Williams and Love’s time with the New York Giants). Love then jokes around saying he needs to sign another contract with Seattle and will retire when Williams does. This heart-felt conversation then goes into discussing what type of boat or truck they need to buy together. Perhaps it can be an ice cream truck – or a mango truck – or an elote truck – maybe a shaved ice truck? It's time for the Hard Knocks season finale 🍿 Stream the new episode now on @hbomax pic.twitter.com/g300DylQKA — NFL (@NFL) September 2, 2026 We are taken along the Jarran Reed “slime-cam” as the Seahawks make their way to Kansas City. Reed is seen calling Sam Darnold “ginger cuz” and telling John Schneider that his shirt is “tighter than a mother f—.” Reed goes from the slime-cam to giving the team a pre-game speech ahead of the final preseason game against the Chiefs. “They brought you here for a reason. Be the reason they brought you here.” Jalen Milroe has a heart-to-heart conversation with his parents ahead of his first full-game action of the season. Trevon Diggs used some of those skills he got playing wide receiver to make this preseason INT 🔥 The season finale of Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @Seahawks is available now on @hbomax pic.twitter.com/hFvhrKNgCQ — NFL (@NFL) September 2, 2026 In the game against the Chiefs , Trevon Diggs uses his wide receiver skills to help him show up with a big interception. Diggs quickly gets the intercepted ball over to his mom in the stands. The Smashing Pumpkins’ “Bullet with Butterfly Wings” song is played over a montage of big plays by the Seahawks, including a big catch by Montorie Foster Jr. However, the reality of the game is shown as well as Mike Macdonald is heard saying “this is the sloppiest game at any level.” On HBO's Hard Knocks .. a convo about the virtual measurement .. Travis Kelce decided to chime in with his thoughts 😂 pic.twitter.com/r2l8VFevvp — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) September 2, 2026 Uso Seumalo gets some pointers from Byron Murphy II and Brandon Pili. Seumalo is also heard telling the referees that the chains are better than the new ball spotting technology. Travis Kelce is overheard agreeing with him – or at least according to Seumalo. Jalen Milroe is seen showing a ton of emotion in response to the offense moving the ball slowly. Coach, Jake Peetz responds to Milroe to “keep imposing confidence in these guys – if they didn’t see you pissed off, they would think something is wrong.” Milroe quickly has a huge throw to Emanuel Henderson Jr. followed by a touchdown throw to Nick Vannett. After the Chiefs game, the attention turns back to the NFL cut-down day. Mike Macdonald reemphasizes to the team in his post-game speech – “It is a 70-man roster … we respect the hell out of you … we are the 2026 Seahawks!” Back at the Virginia Mason Athletic Center, Cooper Kupp is seen talking to some of the players on the roster bubble. Kupp mentions that last year (his first year in Seattle) was the first time that he saw the coaching staff have a true trust in the full 70-man roster to get the job done. Kupp mentions that cut-down day is going to be different than what you are expecting. The infamous cut-down day finally comes. However, it is a lot more joyous than in past…

title: Seahawks Reacts Survey: Who wins on opening night, Seahawks or Patriots?

full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Devon Witherspoon #21 of the Seattle Seahawks forces a fumble against Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots during the fourth quarter in Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. Can you believe it? We’re only eight days away from the Seattle Seahawks opening their 2026 season and unveiling their Super Bowl 60 banner. They will begin their quest for a third Lombardi Trophy with a rematch against the New England Patriots, who had no answers for the Seahawks defense back in February. This might be an “immediate rematch” but it is one in name only. The Patriots significantly retooled their wide receiver room by trading for A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs, added former Seahawk Dre’Mont Jones to the pass rush, and notably brought in veteran safety Kevin Byard. They also signed Alijah Vera-Tucker to help bolster a brutal offensive line. Seattle, of course, is mostly the same team but different in key areas. Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker is now in Kansas City, paving the way for Jadarian Price to become the new face of Seattle’s backfield. Tory Horton should be available for Week 1, whereas Nick Emmanwori isn’t a lock. Ty Okada replaces Coby Bryant, Dante Fowler Jr replaces Boye Mafe, and Nehemiah Pritchett figures to be Riq Woolen’s replacement for now. Oh yes, and there’s a new offensive coordinator in Brian Fleury. New year, same teams, but it’s not the same matchup. Treat it like a new game when the rosters have had enough meaningful change. The survey is simple: Who wins the rematch? You can pick between 1-8 pts or 9+ pts for either team. I think we will tweak the options a little bit moving forward for score predictions but we’ll stick with the classics one more time. There is no “tie” option because, while possible, no one seriously picks NFL football games this way. Association football? Sure. But not gridiron football. Vote in the survey below! full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - AUGUST 15: Noah Igbinoghene #17 of the Seattle Seahawks looks on during the first quarter during the NFL preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys at Lumen Field on August 15, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Any thought of the Seattle Seahawks bringing back Noah Igbinoghene as even a practice squad cornerback can be put on the shelf. The Cleveland Browns have signed Igbinoghene directly to the active roster , as part of a slew of roster transactions they made on Tuesday. Igbinoghene was released as a vested veteran by the Seahawks during final roster cuts and was notably not on the initial practice squad . It seemed like Igbinoghene was in good position to make the active roster after getting a healthy serving of second- and first-team snaps in training camp, along with predominantly second-team snaps in preseason. His first preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys saw him work out of the slot before he was switched the the boundary for the last two games versus the Tennessee Titans and Kansas City Chiefs. For the time being, it looks as if Nehemiah Pritchett is Seattle’s third cornerback on the depth chart, with Trevon Diggs waiting in the wings on the practice squad. Seattle also traded for rookie corner Avery Smith from the Los Angeles Chargers. We’re still unsure as to what future lies ahead for safety D’Anthony Bell, who was part of Seattle’s roster for most of last season before the Carolina Panthers claimed him off waivers. Bell was brought back as a free agent ( with a Super Bowl ring awarded ) and not just cut, but similarly not re-signed to the practice squad.

title: Former Seahawks receivers coach, Super Bowl champion Kippy Brown dies at 71
summary: One of the Seattle Seahawks’ key assistants in their first Super Bowl championship season has passed away. The Knoxville News Sentinel reported on Monday that Kippy Brown, who was Seattle’s wide receivers coach under Pete Carroll from 2010 through the end of the 2014 season, has died at the age of 71. Brown retired from […]
full_text: Feb 2, 2014; East Rutherford, NJ, USA; Seattle Seahawks receivers coach Kippy Brown during Super Bowl XLVIII against the Denver Broncos at MetLife Stadium. The Seahawks defeated the Broncos 43-8. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect One of the Seattle Seahawks’ key assistants in their first Super Bowl championship season has passed away. The Knoxville News Sentinel reported on Monday that Kippy Brown, who was Seattle’s wide receivers coach under Pete Carroll from 2010 through the end of the 2014 season, has died at the age of 71 . Brown retired from coaching after Super Bowl 49. Before Brown coached the likes of Golden Tate, Doug Baldwin, and Jermaine Kearse, he was a groundbreaking football player who was a two-time high school champion and the first Black quarterback in the history of Memphis (then Memphis State) football. The Tennessee native wore many hats on the sidelines as a college and NFL assistant coach, and he was even a head coach for the XFL’s Memphis Maniax in the 2001 season. Throughout his time in the NFL, Brown worked as a running backs coach for three different teams, and served as a wide receivers coach for the Seahawks, Detroit Lions, and Houston Texans. His coaching career began at his alma mater in 1978, when he coached receivers and running backs, plus he had three separate stints as a receivers coach with the Tennessee Volunteers. When Brown retired, his replacement was none other than current Carolina Panthers head coach Dave Canales, who had this to say about his time working alongside Kippy : “I felt very fortunate to be able to have learned from Kippy,” Canales said. “The success that we’ve had, to be able to roll into that with those two years of experience with Kippy, I just feel really comfortable. Then also there’s the (receiver) room; the guys that are here started when I was working with Kippy in 2011, Doug (Baldwin) and Ricardo (Lockette), then Jermaine (Kearse) came the year after that, so I had a chance to work with him. So yeah, I feel a really cool level of comfort with this group, like we grew up together.” And Canales feels like he is prepared for the next step in his career in no small part because of the man he is replacing. “The most important thing that Kippy taught me was just to let the players tell us what they need and what they’re going through,” he said. “At that point in my career in 2011, I was young and hungry and wanted to fix all of a player’s issues in one practice. One of the biggest things is that, with Kip it never felt out of control. With Kip it was like, ‘I’ve seen this before, this is nothing new and it’s going to happen again.'” Coach Carroll also described Brown as, “a lifelong friend” who “played a big-time role in helping our young players and young coaches develop.” A fun fact about Coach Brown is that he once picked up a small role on the big screen. In an interview with the late, great Tony Ventrella back in 2011 , Brown chronicled the time when Oliver Stone asked him if he wanted to be part of the Al Pacino movie, Any Given Sunday . Back then, Brown was Jimmy Johnson’s offensive coordinator with the Miami Dolphins, and he initially was brought over to check the authenticity of the press box set, and “I’m sitting in the press box and [Oliver Stone] says, ‘Well just do what you normally do in the press box.’ So I immediately started ranting and raving and using foul language,” Brown said. “And he said, ‘Tone it down just a little bit.’ By the time we finished I was pantomiming. So I probably talked my way out of a much bigger part.” To give you an idea of how much Kippy Brown meant to his community in Sweetwater, Tennessee, shortly after the Seahawks won Super Bowl 48, Sweetwater High School held a ceremony to name the curved road in the front of the school, “Kippy Brown Way” in honor of their alumnus. Brown was also inducted into the Tennessee Sports Hall of Fame in 2019. RIP Coach Kippy Brown. Our condolences go out to his friends, family, and other loved ones.

title: George Kittle ‘trending in the right direction’ for Week 1
summary: The 49ers’ season opener will be nearly exactly months on from George Kittle tearing his Achilles in their wild-card round win over the Philadelphia Eagles. It appears he will mark the occasion by making his return to the field. Kittle’s status has been one of the big questions hanging over the 49ers ahead of their […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 11: George Kittle #85 of the San Francisco 49ers lines up before the snap during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 49ers’ season opener will be nearly exactly months on from George Kittle tearing his Achilles in their wild-card round win over the Philadelphia Eagles. It appears he will mark the occasion by making his return to the field. Kittle’s status has been one of the big questions hanging over the 49ers ahead of their 2026 season opener against the Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne, Australia. But the star tight end will make the 15-hour journey on Wednesday as the 49ers head Down Under a week early to acclimate to the time difference, with the signs seemingly pointing to him playing at the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground. NFL Network and ESPN’s Ian Rapoport reported early on Wednesday that Kittle has had two positive days of practice and is “trending in the right direction to play”. That would obviously be a massive boost to the 49er offense with everything Kittle brings as both a pass-catcher and as a blocker in the run game. The drop-off in the latter area when he is not on the field has long since been apparent. There is still concern from a defensive perspective concerning Nick Bosa, though Rapoport reported Bosa is “ramping up” his knee as he deals with tendinitis/soreness connected to his ACL reconstruction. Bosa will also make the trip and, for as key as Kittle is the offense, it is arguably more important for the 49ers’ hopes of beating the Rams that the former Defensive Player of the Year is able to get on the field. San Francisco is extremely thin at defensive end. Simply put, they do not have any fearsome outside pass rushers beyond Bosa, and their prospects of generating a pass rush that can help slow down Matthew Stafford and Co. will diminish dramatically if he is not able to play. With Kittle out there, the 49ers have a better chance of keeping up with the Rams in a potential shootout, but they desperately need Bosa to be ready to get the stops they will need to ensure this most arduous of road trips ends in celebration.

title: Grading the 49ers’ initial 53-man roster: Is this a Super Bowl-caliber team?
summary: Now that we’ve had a day or so to process the San Francisco 49ers’ initial 53-man roster and digest the moves that were made, it’s time to evaluate how deep this roster is. Is this a one-and-done playoff team? Can they win the division? Or are we talking about a deep playoff run? Let’s grade the current […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 20: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers throws a pass against the Los Angeles Chargers during the first quarter in a preseason game at SoFi Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images Now that we’ve had a day or so to process the San Francisco 49ers’ initial 53-man roster and digest the moves that were made, it’s time to evaluate how deep this roster is. Is this a one-and-done playoff team? Can they win the division? Or are we talking about a deep playoff run? Let’s grade the current iteration of the 49ers. Quarterbacks (3) Starter: Brock Purdy Backups: Mac Jones, Kurtis Rourke This is the best quarterback room the 49ers have had under Kyle Shanahan. Brock Purdy is the best starter. Mac Jones is the best backup (it was a different Sam Darnold then. And Kurtis Rourke is rookie-year Purdy. The team knowing Rourke wasn’t worth losing on waivers shows foresight into what he means to this team down the line. My not-so-bold prediction is that Purdy plays every game and has a career year. He’ll be playing with the best supporting cast of his life. The wide receivers give Purdy more margin for error than he’s ever had. Plus, quietly, it’s legs should win at least a series-a-game for the offense. Maybe it’s something as simple as escaping a sack and living to fight another down. It very well could mean scrambling for a first down when nothing is there. But I believe the QB tiers from this past offseason will look foolish by season’s end. Grade: A Running backs (4) Starters: Christian McCaffrey, Kyle Juszczyk Backups: Kaelon Black, Jordan James Another strong group for the Niners. Less might be more with Christian McCaffrey early on in the season as the team preserves him for a second-half run. I don’t see a point in giving McCaffrey 30 touches a game in September and October — especially when there are viable options behind him. Reminiscent of 2023, not the version of McCaffrey, but the depth of the running back room. Elijah Mitchell had 75 carries that season. Jordan James had 40 and averaged 5.2 yards per carry. If Kaelon Black and Jordan James can assume that kind of volume, the running game will be potent. Both backups ran well in the preseason. They were decisive, and it led to first downs. Each one of them being able to contribute in the passing game, whether it’s in pass protection or as a receiver, makes it a complete unit. Black and James’ youth will mean inevitable mistakes, but it’s something they’ll need to play through. Grade: A- Wide receivers (6) Starters: Mike Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, Deebo Samuel, Demarcus Robinson Backups: Jordan Watkins, Jacob Cowing The 49ers are expecting Mike Evans back at practice next week as he deals with an adductor injury. The reason it’s easy to be optimistic in the ground game is that safeties can’t hover around the line of scrimmage knowing Evans is lurking on the perimeter. Another reason to be optimistic about the rushing attack is that Evans and Stribling are now the primary blockers. Aaron Donald is objectively one of the best defensive players of this generation. He has not played since 2023. He is 35. Yet, you’d think he’s coming off an All-Pro season the way he’s being discussed. Evans is objectively one of the best wide receivers of this generation. He’s a season removed from missing eight games. Evans is 33. For the previous nine years, 1,000-yard seasons were the norm. Brock is going to have his best season because of Evans. The rushing attack will be at its best because of Evans. Every other receiver on the roster will reap the rewards of Evans. Is there a worry that he’ll miss time? Of course. But with the 49ers’ maintenance plan of not having Evans practice three days in a row, that should aid in keeping Evans available for game days. Stribling gives Purdy his first contested-catch receiver, aside from Evans. While you may think Jauan Jennings was in a similar mode, he was below 50% last season in contested situations. Stribling’s speed was already on full display in the preseason. Deebo will be a jack-of-all-trades. I expect him to live underneath for free access yards. He might be at his best coming out of the backfield as a pass catcher. I saw the results of Evans firsthand and how Robinson got open because of it. I suspect he’ll be Cowing will be the wild card. Best case, Cowing ends up in a Travis Benjamin-esque role from when Shanahan was with the Browns a decade ago. Cowing won’t be a 1,000-yard receiver, but the splash plays will keep the defense honest and the running back will be the beneficiary. Evans is carrying this grade. We live in a world of, “what have you done for me lately?” We forget who Evans is, the situation he’s in, and how athletes generally bounce back and go on a tear when they believe everyone doubts them. Grade: B+ Tight ends (4) Starter: George Kittle Backups: Luke Farrell, Jake Tonges, Brayden Willis Willis making the roster felt like a hedge in case Kittle can’t play right away. Still, keeping a seventh-rounder who has been on and off the roster felt like a risk you didn’t need to take. That’s not to take away from what Willis did in the preseason, but it felt like he would’ve cleared waivers. It’ll be fascinating to see Kittle’s usage coming off an Achilles injury. We know blocking won’t be an issue. But will he be used down the field? Will it matter? Against the Rams linebackers, probably not. Kittle will be 1-on-1 in almost every scenario this season — another way the offense will enjoy the fruits of Evans. It’ll still be a wait-and-see with Farrell. Players tend to improve in Year 2 of Shanahan’s offense. In Farrell’s case, there’s only one direction to go. Tonges is closer to good than average as a receiver, but it’s clear the team doesn’t want him to block. Ideally, we see Tonges more as a receiver, but I’m not holding my breath. Kittle turns 33 in August and is coming off another serious injury. As much as I’d like to give an all-world player the benefit of the doubt, I have to be realistic with him and this group’s expectations. Grade: C+ Offensive line (9) Starters: Trent Williams, Carver Willis**, Jake Brendel, Dominick Puni, Colton McKivitz Backups: Vederian Lowe, Enrique Cruz, Connor Colby, Jarrett Patterson The rookie Willis gets the nod, unless Patterson comes in and steals the show. According to Brandon Thorn’s almanac , the 49ers have the sixth-most experienced unit, with the 11th-most talented. They’re on the older side, ranking 24th—which is saying something, considering a rookie and a third-year pro are starting. He had a fun nugget: The 49ers’ projected line is 33 combined years older than the Dolphins’, while the tackles are the third-lightest starting duo in the league. Willis aside, the continuity is where you want it. We’ll find out if the production follows. Guess who makes the offensive line better? Mike Evans. The blocking shouldn’t be as congested as it was a season ago with a legitimate WR1 who can win outside of the numbers. Quantifying offensive linemen on a down-to-down basis is one of the most difficult things to do in football. They could do their jobs to perfection, but if the quarterback doesn’t get rid of the ball in time, or the running back doesn’t go where he’s supposed to, the line gets assigned the blame. For the longest time, Kyle Shanahan’s offensive lines have been known as the sum being greater than the parts. Despite constant fan blame, I thought the line turned a corner last season. With a better supporting cast, this group will be viewed much more positively this season. Because no one dominates besides Williams, individual matchups are the one area where the line can be susceptible. I mean something along the lines of Myles Garrett versus Colton McKivitz, or Josh Sweat against Carver Willis — the extreme mismatches. As a unit, there are few busted assignments. title: 49ers News: Mike Evans to watch all eight Harry Potter movies on flight to Australia
summary: 49ers wide receiver Mike Evans, at 33, confident he hasn’t lost magic touch (paywall)“Every night, Evans falls asleep to the sounds of the Harry Potter movies playing on the television.  Obsessed with the saga since his second grade teacher read the books to his class about 23 years ago, Evans has watched the films “at […]
full_text: 49ers wide receiver Mike Evans, at 33, confident he hasn’t lost magic touch (paywall) “Every night, Evans falls asleep to the sounds of the Harry Potter movies playing on the television. Obsessed with the saga since his second grade teacher read the books to his class about 23 years ago, Evans has watched the films “at least 1,000 times,” he said. “It comforts me,” Evans said. “It just puts me in a calm state.” It’s not just before bed that Evans incorporates Harry Potter into his life. On his calf is a tattoo of the main character with his best friends, Ron and Hermione. Near his elbow is one of the Deathly Hallows, a symbol key to the series finale. Evans’ 2016 wedding to his wife, Ashli, featured a five-tier cake decorated with all four Hogwarts houses and Hedwig the owl perched in his cage atop. Evans now is starting to get his four young children into the films and books. Evans, 33, doesn’t love the series because of the magic. He loves Harry Potter because of Harry: A kid who loses his parents, grows up with little, discovers his extraordinary talent and is humble despite his status as the chosen one in the wizarding world. “He’s living with his uncle and his cousin, and they treat him like s—. And he’s one of the greatest wizards ever. He’s super humble, competitive. … He’s never too big, even though he is f—ing Harry Potter, the chosen one,” Evans said. “So I’ve always tried to kind of mimic that.” How does he emulate Harry? “He’s just a chill dude, but then he has that fiery side. So I guess I’m kind of similar,” Evans said. “I’m not as great as Harry Potter, but I identify with him.” He plans to watch all the movies on the 16-hour flight to Melbourne…. …He says there’s similarities in competitive fire between Brady and Purdy, but mostly he has noticed how different things are in San Francisco. “This was one of the most competitive camps, if not the most competitive camp, I’ve ever been a part of,” he said. “Everybody’s talking trash to everybody, and it’s good. It’s like, you know, iron sharpens iron. Everybody’s out there just going at each other, trying to make each other better and get each other ready for this long season that we’re about to have.” 49ers’ Raheem Morris shares updates ahead of Australia trip “San Francisco 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris spoke with reporters following Tuesday’s practice as the team prepares to travel to Australia ahead of its Week 1 matchup against the Los Angeles Rams. Here’s everything he had to say.” Kawakami: After a long, weird summer, the 49ers are starting to look whole again (paywall) “The 49ers’ roster is deeper, much more solid, and currently a lot healthier than it was last year, when Shanahan and Lynch decided not to make an all-in move at the trade deadline. (So if this season starts out well — a victory over the Rams would be a big way to get going on that — might Shanahan and Lynch become very interested in pulling off a major trade before the Nov. 10 deadline if they feel they’re just one player away from a Super Bowl run? (And with some depth questions at defensive end, whether or not Bosa is at his best, could that player be Maxx Crosby … if the Raiders’ season turns sour again and they want to trade him … again? Just a thought. That I might be repeating over the next several months.) There are still a lot of question marks heading into Week 1, though. Normal question marks. Are-they-healthy-enough-to-beat-the-Rams question marks. Kittle and Bosa obviously are the two biggest ones. And I think Shanahan and Lynch want them both with the team in Australia for the three practices and all the team meetings.” De’Zhaun Stribling focused on details, changes 49ers jersey to infamous number “I don’t really worry about all the outside noise or the opinions of where I was drafted,” Stribling said. “I’m just here to do my job: catch the ball, score touchdowns and be a great run blocker, also….Details make or break everything,” Stribling said. “Just being on top of the details, being on top of the alignments and assignments. All those kinds of things. It’s much different vs. college.” 49ers traveling to Australia ‘right way’ compared to Rams, per Bay Area coach “I’m not even sure the Rams are going to know what part of the planet they’re on,” Warren told NBC Sports Bay Area. “I’ve done that trip so many times. The first 24, 48, even 72 hours, you’re really struggling with the jet lag. So I’m really surprised to hear that. And, absolutely, the 49ers are doing this the right way.” NBC Sports Bay Area asked McConnell to share his opinions about the differing philosophies based on his experiences of traveling to Australia to play or coach basketball. “The first day is so long,” McConnell said. “If you don’t get good sleep on the plane, you’re just struggling to stay up on day one.” Nick Bosa’s availability remains mystery ahead of 49ers’ trip to Australia (paywall) “Defensive end Keion White doesn’t know whether it’s possible to overdose on melatonin, but he plans on taking five as soon as the plane takes off. If he wakes up? Take five more. “Just keep rolling like that,” White said. Rookie wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling said he’ll watch some TV before attempting to knock out for 10 to 12 hours. Once in Australia, the Hawaii native said he really wants to see a kangaroo. He’s curious how big they are.” Week 2 or 3 debut for Aaron Donald is ‘more likely’ than Week 1 against the 49ers “That’s good news for Carver Willis. The last thing the projected starter at left guard needs is to be made an example out of as Donald proves he’s “still got it” after two years off. Donald won’t be what he once was, but if there’s anybody capable of defying Father Time, he’d be the player to do it.”

title: Week 2 or 3 debut for Aaron Donald is ‘more likely’ than Week 1 against the 49ers
summary: The San Francisco 49ers might have to wait until their second matchup against the Los Angeles Rams to face Aaron Donald. ESPN’s Dan Granziano answered what kind of workload he expects to see from Aaron Donald on Tuesday afternoon: “Well, they’re figuring that out, Laura. He just got there, and he hasn’t played in 2 […]
full_text: SEATTLE, CA - JANUARY 25: Former Rams star Aaron Donald speaks on a telecast before the NFC championship game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026 in Seattle, CA. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) The San Francisco 49ers might have to wait until their second matchup against the Los Angeles Rams to face Aaron Donald. ESPN’s Dan Granziano answered what kind of workload he expects to see from Aaron Donald on Tuesday afternoon: “Well, they’re figuring that out, Laura. He just got there, and he hasn’t played in 2 years. They’re really kind of working him in to practice now, and seeing what, if anything, he’s going to be able to deliver for them. “Remember, their Week 1 game against the 49ers is in Australia, and that game is nine days from today. You can’t rule anything out, obviously, with Aaron Donald. And the Rams aren’t going to rule him out in terms of playing Week 1 — at least not yet. But I would say, based on everything that I’ve been told, a Week 2 or 3 debut looks more likely than Week 1. But again, it’s still on the table. In terms of workload, they’ll watch his snaps, obviously. They have a lot of depth on that defensive line, even just beyond him, in Myles Garrett. They feel like they have the ability early in the season to watch his snaps and count his snaps. As you said, the goal is to win the Super Bowl, not to max him out in Weeks 1, 2, 3.” Even if the 49ers were to face Donald, it’d be on a limited snap count. They won’t complain about not having to game plan for a future Hall of Famer when he’ll be at his freshest and healthiest all season. That’s good news for Carver Willis. The last thing the projected starter at left guard needs is to be made an example out of as Donald proves he’s “still got it” after two years off. Donald won’t be what he once was, but if there’s anybody capable of defying Father Time, he’d be the player to do it.
