title: Life without Myles Garrett: What to expect from Browns defense
summary: Cleveland still expects to field one of the NFL's stingiest defenses -- with a new coordinator, Jared Verse and plenty of returning talent.
full_text:
BEREA, Ohio -- Over the course of a few months, the Cleveland Browns lost two pillars of their elite defense.

 In February, Jim Schwartz, the architect of one of the league's best units over the past three seasons, resigned from his position as defensive coordinator after being passed over for the head coaching job that went to Todd Monken.

 Four months later, the Browns traded defensive end Myles Garrett , the two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and the league's single-season sack leader, to the Los Angeles Rams .

 

 Despite the departures, Cleveland still expects to field one of the stingiest defenses in the NFL -- with a new coordinator in Mike Rutenberg bringing fresh ideas, the 2024 NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year in Jared Verse arriving to lead the pass rush, and plenty of returning talent.

 "I see it as very similar to who we've been in the past," Monken said. "[Rutenberg will] put his own spin on it, and the staff as a collective whole. This is the Cleveland Browns' defense, just like it was last year.

 "Between our staff and 'Rudy' putting together the best plan, almost the same question: what do they believe in, and then what do our players do well? But I see a lot of similar things; we're going to be an attacking-style defense."

 
 Same front, a new leader 
 Well before the Browns entertained the idea of trading Garrett to the Rams, they hired Rutenberg, a former Atlanta Falcons assistant, to keep the foundation of their defense intact: a four-down-linemen scheme with an attacking front.

 Rutenberg, a first-time NFL coordinator, spent a large portion of his coaching career alongside Tennessee Titans coach Robert Saleh, who has used similar defensive fronts as Schwartz did. In 2025, Rutenberg worked with Falcons DC Jeff Ulbrich, another former Saleh assistant.

 Verse, a two-time Pro Bowler who arrived in Cleveland via the blockbuster Garrett trade, steps into the hole vacated by Garrett with his sights on improving from his 12-sack total over his first two seasons.

 Depth along the defensive line has been a concern for the Browns in training camp. Cleveland lost Alex Wright , who was projected to start at defensive end opposite Verse, to a ruptured Achilles two weeks ago . Even before Wright's injury, the Browns had scoured the edge rusher market for depth, hosting veterans Jadeveon Clowney and  Za'Darius Smith  before they signed elsewhere.

 The Browns, though, got much-needed reinforcements last week when linebacker Carson Schwesinger and defensive tackle Maliek Collins returned from injuries that sidelined them for the majority of training camp. Before Collins' season-ending quad injury last December, he was having his most productive season with 6.5 sacks. He returns to the middle of the defense alongside second-year player Mason Graham . The No. 5 overall pick in the 2025 draft, Graham recorded a half-sack as a rookie but was 20th in ESPN's pass rush win rate as an interior defender.

 

 It'll take a collective effort to make up for the NFL-record 23 sacks that Garrett produced last season, but the Browns are hoping it starts with Verse, who already has a reputation for being one of the best bull rushers in the NFL.

 Now the center of a new-look defensive line, Verse told ESPN he learned invaluable lessons from his time with a similarly formidable unit in Los Angeles.

 "The first thing I learned was you can trust your teammates," Verse told ESPN. "You don't got to make every superhero play. You don't got to be that superhero. But then the thing I also learned was to throw that out the window sometimes. Sometimes you have to put that cape back on. Sometimes you got to take those little glasses off and be Superman. You got to make those plays that it might not be your play, but you have to make it.

 "You can't always rely on your teammates, and your teammates can't always just rely on you because sometimes I'm going to mess up, they're going to mess up, and we're going to have to be able to clean each other up."

 
 Changes in the secondary 
 Where Rutenberg will leave his imprint most heavily is on the back end. Already one of the best man coverage secondaries, the Browns are aiming to confuse quarterbacks with increased pre- and post-snap disguises. In Atlanta, Rutenberg was the pass-game coordinator for a defense that was tied for sixth in the league with 16 interceptions last season (Cleveland was tied for 16th with 11).

 Where Garrett acknowledged that Schwartz was almost "stubborn" in his static approach, Rutenberg wants quarterbacks to hesitate by constantly changing what they see before and after the snap. Cleveland disguised its coverage on 19.8% of opponent dropbacks in 2025, which ranked 28th in the league. Atlanta disguised its coverage at a slightly higher rate, 22.9%, which ranked 20th during the same span.

 

 Maybe tellingly, the Browns' defense racked up nearly two dozen interceptions during training camp.

 "I think that this exotic defense that Rudy has, it's a lot of communication," safety Grant Delpit said. "It's a lot of disguise. It's a lot of confusion for the offense."

 And on a defense that already used three-safety lineups frequently, its usage could increase even more after drafting safety Emmanuel McNeil-Warren in the second round of the 2026 NFL draft. Coaches and teammates have raved about McNeil-Warren's athleticism at 6-3 and 210 pounds and the flexibility he could offer on the field -- in pass coverage and run defense.

 Still, Rutenberg doesn't want the essence of a defense that has allowed the fewest yards since 2023 to change. That means, even with the tweaks here and there, playing to his players' strengths, whether it be letting corners Denzel Ward and  Tyson Campbell  play sticky man coverage on an island, or allowing a physical and athletic front to be disruptive and penetrate into the backfield.

 "The key is players," Rutenberg said. "Players make every scheme, whether you're disguised or not, Cover 3, Cover 1, it doesn't matter; everybody runs similar skills. It's about getting guys to understand what we're trying to do, which they've done at the highest level, and giving players opportunities to be successful in whatever coverage or scheme we're in."

title: NFL execs pick snubs in ESPN's 2026 top 100 player rankings
summary: Only 100 players can make our list of the top NFL players for this season. Here are nine who league insiders believe should have been there.
full_text:
The NFL Rank project celebrates 100 players expected to have a terrific season. One problem: More than 100 qualify.

 ESPN's NFL experts rated players based on performance expectations for the 2026 season. Though the players who made the cut are deserving, at least nine marquee players could be classified as snubs -- the most important part of any list, right?

 This project arrives about a month after we finalized our annual positional top 10s project , in which NFL executives, coaches and scouts rank the top players at each position. A review of both rankings shows plenty of similarities in order -- but also a bunch of differences. So, we asked league personnel evaluators to peek at our rankings and nominate players who deserved to be included -- but weren't.

 Note: Commanders offensive tackle Laremy Tunsil was not considered for this exercise due to his recent triceps injury -- again, this is predicting 2026 play. Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald , who came out of retirement Sunday, was also not considered. 

 
 See the full NFL Rank list 

 
 

 

 Baker Mayfield , QB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 Sixteen quarterbacks made this year's top 100, and Mayfield was not one. 

 Mayfield ranks third in passing yards (12,237) and second in touchdown passes (95) since 2023. He has had some success in Tampa Bay, so much so that he turned down a two-year extension of over $100 million in hopes of more long-term security with his team. Mayfield is poised for another big year, which should help his standing on the list.

 "When he's healthy, he's a top-10 quarterback," an NFL personnel evaluator said. "I don't think he was healthy last year. He should have a big season."

 
 

 

 Denzel Ward , CB, Cleveland Browns 
 Ward is, quite comfortably, a top-seven cornerback. This list pushes him out of the top 10.

 "I think durability and the fact he plays in Cleveland keeps him out of the top cornerback discussion, but he's so good," an AFC executive said. "One of the smoothest athletes in all of football."

 Ward typically misses a few games per season because of injury, but his production is undeniable. He has 18 interceptions and 74 pass deflections over eight seasons.

 
 

 Malik Nabers , WR, New York Giants 
 Recovery from a torn ACL affects Nabers' standing. He was limited to 18 catches for 271 yards in four games last season. But when he's healthy, the 23-year-old is easily a top-10 receiver. The top-100 list featured 12 receivers, with Nabers noticeably absent.

 Nabers is one of 10 players all time to record 1,200-plus receiving yards as a rookie (2024).

 "He completely changes the [Giants'] offense if he's healthy this year," an NFC executive said. "It might take him some time, but he moves differently than most receivers when he's full tilt."

 
 

 Kenneth Walker III , RB, Kansas City Chiefs 
 Walker is squarely in his prime (25 years old) without much wear and tear (821 carries in four seasons). He's coming off a dominant three-game playoff stretch, including 313 rushing yards with four touchdowns and a Super Bowl MVP award . And Walker tied for third last season with 10 rushes of at least 20 yards. The other three backs with at least that many -- Jahmyr Gibbs , Derrick Henry and  De'Von Achane  -- ranked in the top 65 of this list.

 "If Andy Reid commits to running the ball, [Walker] is in a position to be a true bell cow who can use his vision to dictate the line of scrimmage," an AFC scout said.

 
 

 

 Brian Branch , S, Detroit Lions 
 Often an underappreciated position, five safeties were featured in this year's NFL Rank. Left off the ballot was Branch, who has established himself as a premier player over the past two seasons with a 1.9% pass breakup percentage that ranks third among safeties. In 2025, Branch was one of two defensive backs with at least five passes defended, five tackles for loss and 2.5 sacks.

 His Achilles tear late last season doesn't help his cause. But the 24-year-old's skill set is undeniable.

 "Really versatile, can put him in the slot or in open space, physical," an AFC personnel evaluator said. "Definitely a top-100 player."

 
 

 Milton Williams , DT, New England Patriots 
 The game is loaded with star defensive tackles -- many of whom make more than $30 million per year. Williams makes $26 million a year, which is a relative bargain for his ability to change games.

 Nine defensive tackles made the top 100 here, and Williams should have been in that group. New England's run defense was drastically improved  with Williams in the lineup. And he had 3.5 sacks and eight tackles for loss over 12 games in 2025.

 "He's a player that's gotten better every year, and he was clearly comfortable being a focal point for the defense," an NFC scout said.

 
 

 Peter Skoronski , G, Tennessee Titans 
 Skoronski is the NFL's highest-paid guard at $25 million annually. But according to NFL Rank, he's not a top-five guard. Chicago's Joe Thuney , Denver's Quinn Meinerz , Indianapolis'  Quenton Nelson , Atlanta's Chris Lindstrom and Dallas'  Tyler Smith round out the top 100 at that position.

 Skoronski has played his way into this conversation and should be on the list next year. He ranked fourth among guards with a 96.0% pass block win rate in 2025.

 "He wasn't a finished product when he came into the league, but he's probably Tennessee's best player on offense, a guy you can build around up front," an NFC exec said. "He's gotten more powerful."

 Kansas City's  Trey Smith was another notable snub at guard.

 
 

 

 Zack Baun , LB, Philadelphia Eagles 
 Baun became an All-Pro and consensus top-five linebacker over the past two seasons in Philadelphia. San Francisco's Fred Warner was the only off-ball linebacker to crack the top 75, and only four made the top 100. Baun has 273 tackles over the past two seasons, along with seven sacks and three interceptions.

 "He's got range. He can play the run close to the box or can cover in space, has great awareness," an NFC executive said. "One of the best at his position."

 
 

 Tucker Kraft , TE, Green Bay Packers 
 Several young tight ends deserve consideration, from Detroit's Sam LaPorta to Indianapolis' Tyler Warren . Let's go with Kraft here because of his upside after  ACL surgery .

 He's a vertical threat who can also block. And by Week 1, he might be the NFL's first $20 million-per-year tight end; the Packers and Kraft are discussing a contract extension.

 "He gives that offense so much juice, and Jordan Love obviously trusts him," an AFC scout said. "If he's healthy, he's primed for a big year."

title: Jahdae Barron waiting his turn in loaded Broncos secondary
summary: Denver's secondary is stacked again, so Barron will once again face a battle to get on the field. But he's set up for 2027 and beyond.
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- Jahdae Barron is clear on the math. Crystal clear.

 Despite being the Denver Broncos ' first-round draft pick in 2025 , the 24-year-old cornerback has been overshadowed -- in playing time, statistical production and in-game impact -- by players drafted before and after him. Such is life when one is dropped into what is arguably the NFL's best secondary.

 But Barron and the Broncos knew this would be the case when he was selected with the 20th overall pick last year. And his confidence regarding what he's capable of this season and beyond has not been dented.

 "You've got to be committed to the process without being emotionally attached to the results," Barron said. "At the end of the day, you wake up and you set goals every day, you just have to keep going ... you can't cheat the process."

 

 Barron's relative lack of playing time as a rookie isn't a deterrent, as he might have played more -- much more -- had he landed with any other NFL franchise. Browns linebacker Carson Schwesinger (No. 33 overall) was selected by a team that's won eight games the past two seasons. He played 956 snaps last season and won the league's Defensive Rookie of the Year award. Nick Emmanwori , picked by the Seahawks two spots after Schwesinger, slid into Seattle's open nickel spot immediately. But Barron joined a Broncos secondary that was already stacked with quality starters and returns each of those players this season.

 Included are two players, cornerback Pat Surtain II and safety Talanoa Hufanga , who earned second-team All-Pro honors last season. They are joined by fourth-year cornerback Riley Moss -- who Hufanga has called "one of the most athletic corners I've ever been around" -- safety Brandon Jones and nickel corner Ja'Quan McMillian , considered by many evaluators to be one of the best nickels in the league.

 Those players helped the Broncos' pass defense finish first in the NFL in yards allowed per dropback (4.95) and second in the NFL in completion percentage allowed (57.8%) and yards allowed per pass attempt (6.1). So Barron is combination of philosopher, dreamer and old-school grinder with his own way to measure progress.

 "People have opinions and whatever the opinions, it truly doesn't matter," Barron said. "I'm going to wake up and eat the same exact food ... I'm going to text my mom. ... Nothing changes about my life ... I'm just going to continue meet my expectations and not somebody else's expectations."

 Those expectations could collide with increased playing time soon. Moss, McMillian and Jones are poised to be on a hearty list of Broncos scheduled to be unrestricted free agents next March. Moss and McMillian took similar paths to what Barron is taking, which the former first-rounder acknowledges.

 "As humans we want more, and we try and beat and rush the process," Barron said. " ... You just have to stay true to what you believe in and sometimes it's hard. Sometimes you won't wake up in the mood, it won't be your day, but at the end of the day, you've got to be strong."

 

 He has a high bar to clear for more playing time in the short term. Surtain was voted as the best cornerback in the league in an ESPN poll of coaches, scouts and league personnel executives. Moss is the most challenged man-to-man cornerback in the league because of Surtain's presence and possesses the kind of athleticism and competitiveness the Broncos want opposite the All-Pro.

 But Barron is doing his part to make his case for more playing time in 2026 and down the road. He returned an interception 97 yards for a touchdown in the preseason opener against the Falcons. He is also one of the fastest players in the league (he ran a 4.39 40-yard dash at the 2025 combine at 194 pounds), and his positional versatility allows him to move around the defense.

 Barron is also known as a sure tackler, with several league personnel executives saying he didn't miss one in his final season at Texas. That gave the Broncos the liberty to play him at outside corner, nickel corner, safety and as a linebacker in the team's dime package (six defensive backs) last season, a menu that should be similar this year.

 "He wants more, obviously, I want more for him," Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph said. " ... But I've said, we have a good secondary, and for us to have three or four or five good corners, that's a good thing, not a bad thing ... It's about finding those places where he can help us."

 That won't involve a position move, as Broncos coach Sean Payton has made it clear that cornerback will be Barron's primary job.

 

 "I read somewhere where we moved him to safety ... I'm not [moving him]," Payton said. "He's playing nickel, he's playing corner and then when we get into dime, he replaces a linebacker. So, he's doing really good."

 Assuming the Broncos stay healthy, 2026 might not see a big uptick of snaps for Barron. But he believes all the multi-tasking is good for the long game of his career.

 "Once you're at so many different positions, it allows you to understand everybody else's job ... and when you know everybody else's job, it allows you to know what kind of leverage you're supposed to be in," Barron said. "Right now it's still working parts, working movements, but I look down the line and it's going to be amazing."

title: What will Packers get from Kaleb Johnson, Jonnu Smith?
summary: The three newest Packers won't have much time to get their bearings before Week 1 kicks off against the Vikings.
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- They insist it wasn't planned, but the three newest members of the Green Bay Packers -- tight ends Jonnu Smith and Mark Redman and running back Kaleb Johnson -- were lined up side by side by side in warmups before the first practice with their new team Tuesday.

 "I guess the new guys are trying to figure it out," Smith said.

 Perhaps more importantly, it's coach Matt LaFleur and offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich who need to figure out how quickly -- and how much -- the trio can contribute when the season opens on Sept. 13 at the Minnesota Vikings .

 None of the three will have to be the primary player at his position, but the Packers could use at least some help from all of them.

 

 Johnson, who was acquired Sunday in a trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers for a sixth-round pick in 2028, joins a backfield that is filled with uncertainty. The Packers won't have their top running back, Josh Jacobs , who is on the commissioner exempt list while his legal situation plays out.

 The rest of the running back group includes MarShawn Lloyd , the former third-round pick who has played in one game over two NFL seasons, third-down pass protector Chris Brooks and practice squad member Pierre Strong Jr .

 While the Packers may have stopped holding their breath about whether Lloyd can stay healthy -- by making it through training camp unscathed, he has put together the longest stretch of good health since he came into the league in 2024 --  it's not like they're going to suddenly give a guy who has six career NFL carries a Jacobs-like workload.

 "That's to be determined," LaFleur said of Lloyd on Tuesday. "Who knows? I couldn't tell you right now, so we'll see how he's feeling. He's had a really steady camp. I think he did an outstanding job. Obviously his availability has been critical, and we'll just see how it goes."

 

 Johnson had 28 carries as a rookie last season for the Steelers. The third-rounder's most notable play was a botched kickoff return in Week 2, when he let a live ball bounce past him and into the end zone, where the Seahawks recovered it for a touchdown.

 LaFleur and general manager Brian Gutekunst both mentioned how well Johnson performed in college at Iowa and noted that it's a similar scheme to what the Packers run. Iowa offensive coordinator Tim Lester spent a season on LaFleur's staff in Green Bay before going to the Hawkeyes.

 "Kaleb's a guy that we really liked coming out of Iowa," LaFleur said. "I've talked to Tim Lester about him a little bit. Certainly I think he's really good at the outside zone stuff. ... He's a young, talented player.

 "We're excited to get him in here and certainly he's got a lot to learn in terms of how we go about everything and from a schematic standpoint, making sure he's dialed in, not only in our run game but obviously in the passing game, as well, whether it's protections or his route assignment."

 At tight end, half the position group just joined the team in the past week.

 The Packers agreed to terms with Smith on Thursday. To start the first team meeting with Smith in Green Bay, LaFleur introduced him.

 "I'm like trying to look where he's sitting; he's sitting right next to [quarterback]  Jordan Love ," LaFleur said. "I'm like, that's a vet move, so he knows how to work it."

 

 The veteran spent last season with the Steelers but also spent one year with LaFleur in Tennessee in 2018, when LaFleur was the Titans' offensive coordinator.

 "I only had him that one year and, obviously, he was able to know my talents and my capabilities and my abilities," Smith said of LaFleur. "I was kind of in this system that he's established offensively for a while now in my career. So that also played into account of my decision of coming here."

 Redman, who was acquired in a trade Sunday from the Los Angeles Rams for a seventh-round pick in 2028, also has some indirect connection to the Packers' offense. He played last season for the Rams. LaFleur and Rams coach Sean McVay are not only close friends but also run a similar offense.

 "[LaFleur's] brother was there last year, Mike; now I'm here with him and I know they've been together for quite a handful of years on and off," Redman said. "Got here and [tight ends coach John Dunn] started talking about the offense and I was like, 'Wait, I know that play [and] I know that play.'

 "Obviously there's going to be some new stuff, but whatever package they're going to use me in and getting my hand in the dirt, a lot of it's carryover, so it's pretty nice to be able to go out there and play Day 1. Super helpful."

 At least the Packers still have starting tight end Tucker Kraft , even if it's on a snap limit since he hasn't played in a game since sustaining an ACL tear on Nov. 2. Both he and the Packers have tried to get a contract extension done before Week 1 but have yet to come to terms. Kraft, however, said that won't keep him from playing.

 "I will be on the field to play for the Green Bay Packers, regardless of any contract situation, because I love this team," Kraft said.

title: Travis Kelce reveals his and Taylor Swift's dog to the world
summary: The dog, a female Samoyed, starred alongside Kelce in an ad campaign for Tommy Hilfiger.
full_text:
The house of Kelce-Swift has found its royal pet.

 On Tuesday, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce revealed his dog to the world in a Tommy Hilfiger campaign. The dog, a female Samoyed, is seen hanging out alongside Kelce as he makes his way through New York's Plaza Hotel while Ace Frehley's cover of "New York Groove" plays.

 

 When the Tommy Hilfiger team wanted a dog in the ad campaign, Kelce suggested his own, according to Vogue .

 "We figured, why not her?" Kelce told Vogue. "She crushed it, and actually really fit into that Tommy aesthetic, too. Those are some of my favorite shots."

 Carmelo Anthony, tennis star Frances Tiafoe, Blackpink singer Jisoo, model Gigi Hadid and singer Peggy Gou are also featured in the ad. Vogue reports the collaboration between Hilfiger and Kelce will be available summer 2027.

 Kelce is preparing for his 14th and potentially final season in the NFL. His marriage earlier this year to pop superstar Taylor Swift at Madison Square Garden was attended by dozens of celebrities , from his teammate Patrick Mahomes to Mariska Hargitay to Paul Rudd.

title: How the Los Angeles Rams got Aaron Donald back
summary: It was a conversation coach Sean McVay never expected to have with the 10-season vet, but three months later, Donald is back in a Rams uniform.
full_text:
LOS ANGELES -- It was late May when Sean McVay called Aaron Donald .

 McVay and the Los Angeles Rams were considering trading for reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett , and the Rams' head coach was curious what Donald thought of the idea.

 Donald, who retired in March 2024 at age 32, is "a close friend of mine," McVay said, and as a former player has a "great perspective on how we operate."

 Not only did Donald like the idea of the team acquiring Garrett, but he also realized, "I wish I was still out there playing right about now." 

 "Seeing what was being done with this team, the pieces that were getting brought here," Donald said. "I was like, 'OK, it's a complete team.' And then you see other moves they [made]."

 On June 1, the Rams traded for Garrett, sending outside linebacker Jared Verse to the Cleveland Browns as part of a package that included a first-round pick in 2027 and a second-round pick in 2028.

 

 When Donald mentioned the idea of coming out of retirement to McVay, it led to a conversation the head coach never expected to have. 

 "When he sat down with me and he said, 'I'm full, I'm complete,' he meant it and I believed him," McVay said in late July. "I think out of respect for him, you don't revisit those things."

 Donald had retired after 10 NFL seasons as a three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and an eight-time first-team All-Pro.

 While there was no doubt in McVay's mind that Donald would impact the defense if he returned, he also wanted to make sure Donald knew he didn't owe the organization anything. As McVay fielded questions about Donald's potential return throughout training camp, he reiterated that Donald had earned the right to make a decision on his own timeline.

 Three months after the pair had their first conversation about the possibility of Donald coming out of retirement, Donald and the Rams agreed to a one-year, $20 million deal with playoff incentives that can raise the total value of the deal to $30 million, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. It took what Donald called "a long process," one that general manager Les Snead described to Pat McAfee on Monday as "a grueling summer." Now, the Rams might be positioned to have the best defensive front in NFL history, in part because of the addition of Garrett and the relationship McVay has with Donald.

 "I mentioned to Sean [McVay] yesterday," Snead told McAfee . "For a player of his caliber to want to leave retirement and probably what -- two, three years away from a first-ballot, possibly Hall of Fame moment to go, you know, I'll put that on hold to come and play for you. I think their relationship is special."

 

 

 IT WASN'T LONG after that late-May conversation with McVay that Donald started putting himself in a position to train and get his body to the point that he could see how he felt, how he moved and whether he could play again in the NFL -- now at age 35 -- and at the All-Pro level he was accustomed to.

 
For the past 14 weeks, Donald said, he put himself through "nonstop grinding" to get to the point he could potentially return to the practice field in late August. McVay described the work as a "very strict, regimented process" similar to what the defensive tackle went through as a player.

 Although he hadn't played football for two years, Donald said he lifted weights and worked on his conditioning. "It was a little different transition into the grass again, running [and] cutting," he said. 

 Donald said Sunday he didn't know how his preparation would translate, but on Aug. 9, the first day he worked with his speed trainer who had trained him since high school, he got good news.

 

 "He looked at me and said, 'You ain't missed a step,'" Donald said. "That's why it was important for me to work with a guy that knows me, that's been around me since day one, since high school. Just to get his advice of how I'm looking, what he's thinking. Obviously over time, I got better, got a little quicker. I started feeling better, the second wind started kicking in a little differently. After you get to that point, that second wind kicks in, now it's time to transition and start doing some football stuff.

 "A long process, but it was my process that I needed to do to make myself feel like I can do it."

 Donald said he was "on and off" on whether to return during the past couple of months of training. His wife, Erica, was on board, telling him, "If you want to do this, [I'm] with [you] 100%." And although there were days Donald doubted he should come back, she told him not to rush things.

 "You want to do this," she told him. "Don't make no decisions faster than what you need to make a decision. Take your time."

 And then, in mid-August, Donald had made up his mind.

 "I talked to Sean [McVay] every single week, damn near every day," Donald said. "We stayed in contact. I gave him all my updates, how I was feeling, how things were going. I know he got annoyed with [media] asking all the questions in camp every damn day. I felt bad for him at that point, but I was doing everything I needed to do to give myself peace of mind and see if I can do it.

 "[There] wasn't [any] rushing. I just wanted to take my time and make the right decision because once you choose to come back, you're all the way back in. You can't be halfway in; you [have to] be all the way in it. I had to get to that point where I felt like I'm 100% committed to playing football again because the last two years have been amazing."

 

 

 DURING THAT PROCESS , the Rams opened training camp on July 26 at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles. The day before the first practice, Rams defensive line coach Giff Smith sat down with his position group one-on-one to be "open and honest" about the possibility of Donald returning and what that would mean for those players. Earlier that day, McVay also addressed the possibility of adding Donald to the team in his first news conference of training camp.

 "We did individual meetings, and they deserve the right to ask and understand and create clarity because the unknown is what bothers people," Smith said. "And so we had a good discussion, aired it all out, and then I told them then we're going to work the next day.

 "And so thought it was beneficial for everybody and it really kind of cleared the air and we could just go to work and have a good training camp."

 Defensive end Braden Fiske , who was drafted at No. 39 by the Rams a month after Donald retired, said while he thought Smith's update "was needed to just address the situation that was going on," he "didn't think too much of it past that."

 "It was one conversation and back to work," Fiske said. "I wasn't going to let something like that hinder how I go about my business on the field or off the field, and I was just going to keep working and keep fighting. And that's what we've done so far. And it's worked out up to now."

 

 Fiske said Smith is a coach who likes to rotate his players in and out of games and that "the cool thing about our room is we're comfortable rolling with anybody on the field."

 And while Donald said Sunday that he hopes the defense can "do some special things together," he is also aware the Rams had a "complete" team before he came out of retirement.

 "I already thought it was a stacked D-line ... then you bring a guy like Myles Garrett, a generational talent, and [I was] like, 'That can be fun,'" Donald said. "Obviously, what they did on the back end, bringing certain pieces they need at the secondary, I think this is a complete team with me here or without me here. So for me to even have the opportunity to be a part of this, be with this team, I take nothing for granted.

 "It's a blessing to be retired from the game for two years and have the opportunity to come back and be a part of something special. Nothing is promised, nothing is guaranteed, but I'm trying to get to that ultimate goal day by…

title: Odell Beckham Jr. reclaims iconic No. 13 jersey with Giants
summary: The star wide receiver is returning to the number he wore during his first stint in New York from 2014 to 2018.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- New York Giants fans can pull those No. 13 jerseys out of the closet. They're officially back in circulation for star wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr .

 After making the 53-man roster over the weekend, Beckham was back on the field Tuesday in his trademark No. 13. It just looked right.

 Beckham wore No. 3, his high school and college number at LSU, throughout the spring and summer with the Giants. He reclaimed No. 13 on Tuesday from fellow wide receiver Jalin Hyatt , who is on the practice squad.

 On Tuesday morning, Beckham posted an Instagram story of the No. 13 jersey with his name on the back sitting on his stool in the locker room. It was a full-circle moment.

 

 Hyatt gave up the number without hesitation. It was always the plan assuming both receivers made it to this point and Beckham had a spot on the roster.

 Hyatt was on the practice field Tuesday wearing No. 81.

 It was known from the day that Beckham signed with the Giants in the spring this was the likely outcome. No. 3 was always a placeholder. That number was already being worn by second-year outside linebacker Abdul Carter .

 Beckham said Monday there would be a "conversation" about returning to the number he wore during his first stint in New York from 2014 to 2018. He made three straight Pro Bowls to start his career while making the No. 13 Giants jersey famous.

 

 "I think we all know what that means to me, and there definitely will be some conversations," Beckham said. "I'll just say we'll see what happens, but like I said, it would be an honor and a privilege to put that back on."

 That's exactly what ended up happening. Now, Beckham will be coming out of the tunnel in No. 13 for the Giants' season opener Sept. 13 against the Dallas Cowboys , the team that witnessed many of his old highlights. Surely there will be plenty of No. 13 Beckham jerseys in the stands.

 "I would say it's pretty nostalgic," quarterback Jaxson Dart said. "Just, as a kid, that's like an icon, in a way where you feel like he changed the game a little bit. You're in your backyard as a young kid, talking about Odell when you catch it one hand, or just things like that. So, that part, it's a really cool experience."

title: Why the Titans are betting on Cam Ward heading into Year 2
summary: Tennessee's newest coach and new offensive coordinator Brian Daboll are helping to elevate the second-year QB.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- Few things will have more impact on the Tennessee Titans ' ability to able to turn things around than second-year quarterback  Cam Ward 's continued development under new offensive coordinator Brian Daboll.

 Ward didn't do much to generate excitement in two preseason games, but he's shown flashes during joint practices with the Seattle Seahawks and Chicago Bears . Titans coach Robert Saleh, who stepped into the role this offseason after Brian Callahan was fired after a 1-5 start last year, is convinced Ward is ready to lead Tennessee to big things.

 Saleh is so convinced, he's betting his job on it.

 "This kid's not going to fail," Saleh said Sunday. "Obviously, I put my job on that one, but he's not going to fail. He's special."

 

 With Ward guiding the way, the Titans reached the end zone on only one of their six preseason drives, but Saleh said he puts more stock in joint practices than in preseason games -- at least that's how he feels for guys like Ward, who already have a secure roster spot and get to execute more scheme-based reps.

 Ward explained why joint practice has been more effective for the offense than preseason games.

 "During practice we're doing more game stuff that we do in a real football game," Ward said after joint practice with the Bears. "It's a lot of stuff that we don't want to put on tape by showing in the preseason game. So practice is more of getting better at the stuff we know we're going to do come Week 1, Week 2 and Week 3.

 "It's a difference when you know the certain types of plays that we're putting in each week."

 In a season where the Titans finished 3-14 for the second straight year, Ward finished last with 3,169 passing yards (17th), 15 touchdowns (25th) and seven interceptions (tied for 10th most). He completed 59.8% (33rd) of his passes but showed signs over the final five games by posting eight touchdown passes and only being intercepted once. Daboll is looking to extrapolate the latter success over the course of a full season.

 "I have a lot of confidence in this young man," Daboll said. "I have confidence in how he played [in college] at Miami and Washington State, and he had a whole year under his belt in the National Football League and getting accustomed to the speed of the game and the timing. That's not an easy thing for quarterbacks."

 

 What the Titans staff wants Ward to do 

 Daboll and quarterbacks coach Shea Tierney are not looking to tweak Ward's throwing motion, but they do want to streamline his decision making, encouraging him to take what the defense gives him while still hunting for opportunities to generate chunk plays. Ward is, in essence, being asked to manage the game, which isn't a bad thing.

 "With Cam, his job is to lead the offense and make good decisions with the football," Daboll said. " To get us out of bad plays if we don't have the right look, to make the right decisions on a play-by-play basis."

 There will be opportunities to take shots down the field, but Daboll's scheme intends to use the short passing game to set it up. There's always been an emphasis on the slot receiver under Daboll. That's why the team signed  Wan'Dale Robinson  to a four-year, $70 million deal in March. It's also why a quicker, slimmed-down version of Xavier Restrepo made the initial 53-man roster.

 

 Daboll is relying on Ward reading the defense to determine where to go with the football. The emphasis is on Ward having his "eyes in the right spot" and "being able to move defenders when we need to move them."

 There will be times where Ward is expected to hold the safety on one side of the field with his eyes to open up a window to deliver the ball down the field on a post or seam route. That's when Ward has the green light to go hunting for a big play.

 Situational awareness is another trait Daboll and the staff are focusing on improving for Ward. Red zone, two-minute and third-down periods emphasize taking care of the ball and not making reckless decisions.

 The Titans needed an average of 7.2 yards to pick up a first down on third down last season -- tied for the eighth-highest distance in the NFL. That was a big factor in finishing second to last with a 31.9% conversion rate and averaging a league-worst 3.7 third-down conversions per game.

 "Our goal for training camp is being efficient on first and second down," Ward said. "Stay out of third-and-long, because in third-and-5 or less, you pretty much know what they can play. They can still do something different. But when you get into third-and-6, third-and-7 to 10 plus, that's when you got to really key in on your protections.

 "It's going to be deeper dropbacks. They know it's a dropback pass, so you're really playing at the defense's advantage."

 Why there's hope 

 Daboll is taking the same approach to Ward as he did to a young Josh Allen back in 2018 with the Buffalo Bills . The first step this offseason was getting to know each other as men. From there it turned to seeing the game through the eyes of Ward and getting him to see things from the playcaller's perspective as well.

 Understanding the why makes it easier to execute what the play is designed to accomplish.

 "I think Cam has really grasped what we want to do, and we just got to continue to build and work on the execution part of it," Daboll said.

 Now the Titans' attention will turn to game planning for the New York Jets for next week's season opener, with Ward's final practice of camp being highlighted by three touchdown passes, including two to No. 4 overall pick Carnell Tate .

 Ward has started to feel more comfortable executing the offense and is able to adjust on the fly, as well.

 "Everything slowed down," Ward said. "We're finally at the point where we're not going to be installing too much stuff. One thing about coach [Daboll] is he can go to walkthrough, he can make up a play in his head, and we'll run it right there and we will execute it right there. So it's going to be nice to really show what we really are about when the time comes."

 The joint practice with Chicago was a reminder of what an offense looks like when a playcaller/quarterback relationship goes right. In his first year, coach Ben Johnson helped catapult quarterback Caleb Williams and the Bears to an 11-6 record and an NFC North title last season after Williams went 5-12 as a rookie.

 

 Williams, a fellow No. 1 overall pick, knows what it's like to be in Ward's shoes.

 "[Daboll] has been an awesome offensive coordinator in this league for a while now," Williams said. "He has good track record with quarterbacks. Just believe and trust in him; what he's coaching and teaching you. Then it's just go execute. We have some similarities in our game in being able to make the big plays, but keep consistently making the small plays."

 Ward placed trust in Daboll from Day 1 because he was intentional about discovering what Ward liked, and he immediately implemented it into the game plan.

 "That showed me he's willing to at least listen to me," Ward said." He knows who he has at quarterback. I trust him and he trusts me."

 Reason for concern 

 All of the synergy sounds good on the surface, but the facts are the facts, with Ward completing 13 of 24 passes for 126 yards in two preseason games.

 He struggled to connect on deep passes, missing all seven of his attempts over 10 yards. Not all of it has been on Ward though.

 Tate failed to haul in a well-placed over the shoulder throw along the sideline in the Seattle game. Tight end Gunnar Helm failed to get his feet in bounds after Ward extended the play and found him in an open area as he scrambled against the Seahawks.

 

 Daboll pointed out how intermediate chunk passing plays, that can be layered throws or man-to-man throws "encompass everybody" to execute properly.
